name: How Objects Become Icons: Photography, Publishing and the Making of Design History
description:
Studio Ballo+Ballo, 1954, Divano D70, Osvaldo Borsani for Tecno
Join us for a talk with historian and curator Libby Sellers exploring how twentieth-century design became iconic not simply through the objects themselves, but through the visual ecosystems that surrounded them: photography, magazines, catalogues, advertising, exhibitions, museums and collecting. 

Beginning with John Berger’s Ways of Seeing and the idea that every image embodies a particular way of seeing, the talk considers how images have shaped our understanding of what design looks like, what it means, and which objects and designers become part of the cultural canon.

From post-war Italian design through Californian architecture, it asks how photography transforms both the built environment and our understanding of it. The talk then brings this framework into a South Asian context through the architect Minnette de Silva and the journal MARG, exploring the role of publishing in making a regional modernism visible and intelligible, while opening questions around gender, authorship and the construction of the design canon. Drawing on research into twentieth-century furniture, women designers and collectible design, the talk asks who gets photographed, published, collected and remembered, and who remains outside the frame. 

Ultimately, the talk asks: when we think we recognise an iconic object, are we recognising the object itself, or the history of images that has taught us how to see it?
